title: Legal, Ethical & Regulatory Considerations
description: Know the legal, ethical and regulatory rules every media creator must follow before publishing.
content_html:
Why Law and Ethics Matter in Media

Creating a media product does not happen in a vacuum. Every piece of content — a photograph, a music track, a piece of writing, a video clip — may be protected by law, subject to industry regulation or carry ethical responsibilities to the audience it reaches. Professional media creators must understand these obligations before they begin production, not after. Failing to do so can result in legal action, financial penalties, reputational damage or harm to the people depicted in the product.

Copyright and Intellectual Property

Copyright is the most important legal concept for media creators. It exists automatically when an original work is created — a photograph, a piece of music, a written article or a film — and gives the creator (or whoever owns the copyright) the exclusive right to control how that work is used. Using someone else's copyrighted material without permission is an infringement and can lead to legal action. Intellectual property is the broader category that includes copyright, trademarks (protecting brand names and logos) and patents (protecting inventions). Media creators must be able to demonstrate that every asset in their product is either their own original work, properly licensed, or covered by an appropriate usage right.

Key Fact

Copyright protects original creative works automatically from the moment of creation. In the UK, copyright in a photograph, film or written work typically lasts for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years. After this period, the work enters the public domain and can be used freely.

Licensed, Royalty-Free and Creative Commons Assets

When a media creator needs to use an asset they did not create — a stock photograph, a music track, a font — they have several legal options. A licensed asset requires the creator to seek formal permission from the copyright holder, often paying a fee. Royalty-free assets can be purchased for a one-off payment and then used without paying ongoing royalties every time the product is published or broadcast. Creative Commons (CC) licences are a standardised set of permissions granted by the copyright holder. A CC BY licence allows use as long as the creator is attributed; CC BY-NC adds the restriction that the work cannot be used for commercial purposes; CC BY-ND prohibits creating adapted versions. Public domain works have no copyright restrictions — either the copyright has expired or the creator has waived all rights. Choosing the right type of asset is a legal obligation, not merely a best practice.

If a media product features identifiable people — whether in photographs, video footage or named in text — the creator must obtain the appropriate permissions. A model release is a signed agreement from a person confirming that their image can be used in a specific way (e.g. in an advert). A location release grants permission to film or photograph on private property. Without these, the creator could face claims under privacy law or data protection legislation. In the UK, the Data Protection Act 2018 and the UK GDPR govern how personal data — including photographs that identify individuals — can be collected and used. Media creators working with children must also ensure parental consent is obtained before recording or publishing any content featuring under-18s.

Regulation and Age Ratings

The media industry is regulated by both government bodies and independent organisations to ensure content is appropriate for its intended audience. PEGI (Pan European Game Information) provides age ratings for video games: PEGI 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. These ratings are based on content analysis covering violence, language, sexual content, gambling and drug use, and are legally enforceable in the UK for the 12, 16 and 18 categories — retailers must not sell age-restricted games to younger buyers. The BBFC (British Board of Film Classification) classifies films for cinema and home release with ratings including U (suitable for all), PG (parental guidance), 12A/12, 15 and 18. (12A is the cinema certificate — under-12s may watch with an adult — while 12 is the equivalent for home video/DVD, where no one under 12 is admitted.) Like PEGI 12+ ratings, BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 certificates carry legal force for cinema admissions.

Key Fact

PEGI rates video games with five age categories: 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. The BBFC classifies films with: U, PG, 12A/12, 15 and 18. PEGI 12, 16 and 18 ratings are legally enforceable in UK retail; BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 certificates are legally enforced for cinema admission.

Students frequently mix up PEGI and BBFC, or claim that all ratings are "just a recommendation". PEGI rates games (not films); the BBFC rates films (and video works). Both systems have legally enforceable elements: PEGI 12, 16 and 18 are enforceable at UK retail points of sale; BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 certificates are enforced at UK cinemas. PEGI 3 and 7, and BBFC U and PG, are advisory rather than legally enforced. In an exam, state which body rates which type of product, name the specific rating categories, and distinguish between advisory and legally enforced ratings — this level of precision is what takes an answer to Mastering.

Ethical Considerations in Media

Beyond legal obligations, media creators must consider the ethical impact of their work — particularly in how people are represented. Stereotyping is the use of oversimplified or inaccurate generalisations about groups of people. Repeated stereotyping in media can reinforce prejudice and cause real harm to the groups depicted. Ethical creators consider whether their content fairly represents people of different genders, ethnicities, ages, abilities and backgrounds. Related concerns include offensive content (material that demeans or dehumanises individuals or groups), privacy (filming or publishing images of people without consent), and the accuracy of information presented as factual. Ethical responsibilities extend to online content: using photoshopped imagery without disclosure, or creating misleading advertising, are both legal and ethical concerns even when technically permitted.
exam_tip_html: For legal and regulatory questions, precision is essential. Always name the correct body (PEGI for games, BBFC for films) and the specific rating categories — never write "the ratings board" generically. When discussing copyright, distinguish between the type of licence: "royalty-free" is not the same as "copyright-free" or "free to use". For ethics questions, name a specific concern (stereotyping, privacy, representation) and explain both what it is and why it matters to the audience or the individuals depicted, not just that "it could cause offence".
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Copyright protects original creative works automatically; media creators must ensure every asset is their own, properly licensed, Creative Commons-approved or in the public domain — using copyrighted material without permission is an infringement.
  • PEGI rates video games (3, 7, 12, 16, 18) and the BBFC rates films (U, PG, 12A/12, 15, 18); PEGI 12, 16 and 18 and BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 are legally enforced, while lower categories are advisory.
  • Ethical responsibilities include avoiding harmful stereotyping, respecting privacy, obtaining model and location releases, and ensuring content accurately represents the people and facts it depicts.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal right of a creator to control how their original work is used, copied, distributed or adapted, which exists automatically when a work is created.
The legal rights that protect creations of the mind, including copyright, trademarks and patents.
The Pan European Game Information system, which classifies video games with age ratings (3, 7, 12, 16 and 18) to help consumers and parents make informed choices.

practice_questions.text:
Which organisation provides age ratings for video games sold in the UK?
A) BBFC
B) Ofcom
C) PEGI
D) ASA
State two types of asset licence that allow a media creator to use material they did not create.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct answers, for example: royalty-free licence [1]; Creative Commons licence [1]; commercially licensed/permission-based licence [1]; public domain (no licence required) [1]. Answers must name a specific licence type; "stock images" alone scores zero without specifying the licence. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a Creative Commons (CC) licence and give one example of how it restricts use.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a Creative Commons licence lets you use someone else's work'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'a Creative Commons licence is a standardised set of permissions granted by the copyright holder that allows others to use the work under defined conditions without seeking individual permission'). A fully developed answer with a specific restriction scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'for example, a CC BY-NC licence allows use of the work as long as the original creator is attributed and the work is not used for any commercial purpose — so a student could use it in a school project but a company could not use it in a paid advertisement'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a PEGI rating and a BBFC certificate. Give one example of a rating from each system.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): PEGI is the Pan European Game Information system and classifies video games; the BBFC (British Board of Film Classification) classifies films and video works for cinema and home release. Both systems use age-based categories, but PEGI applies specifically to games and the BBFC to films (2 marks for a clear distinction naming both bodies and their scope; 1 mark for identifying only one).
Examples (1 mark each): PEGI example — e.g. a PEGI 16 rating means the game is not suitable for players under 16 and is legally enforced at UK retail; BBFC example — e.g. a BBFC 15 certificate means only those aged 15 and over may see the film at a UK cinema, and this is legally enforced. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A media student is producing a short documentary about life in their local town. They plan to film people in a shopping centre, use a popular song as background music and include photographs they found on an image-sharing website.

Discuss the legal and ethical considerations the student must address before publishing the documentary.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two distinct legal or ethical issues, applied to the scenario. For example: copyright in the popular music track requires a licence — the student cannot simply use a chart song without permission or payment, and must source a royalty-free or Creative Commons alternative; the photographs from the image-sharing website require checking the licence attached to each image (CC licence terms or royalty-free status). Ethical dimension: filming identifiable people in the shopping centre without consent raises privacy concerns, and publishing their images could require model releases. Both issues should be developed with reasoning and scenario application.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two issues identified and briefly explained with some scenario reference.
Developing (2 marks): One issue identified with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague point about legal issues with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A games developer has created a first-person action game that features realistic violence and strong language. The developer believes age ratings are an unnecessary restriction on creative freedom and that players should decide for themselves what content is appropriate.

Evaluate the extent to which age ratings such as PEGI benefit both the games industry and its audiences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues age ratings benefit the industry by providing clear, trusted guidance to parents and consumers (reducing returns and complaints), protecting the industry from government censorship by demonstrating self-regulation, and enabling developers to create adult content for adult audiences without fear of the whole market being restricted; then challenges this by engaging with the developer's counter-argument that ratings can restrict creative expression, create commercial barriers for smaller studios who cannot afford classification fees, and that digital distribution (direct download, streaming) makes enforcement increasingly difficult. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about the overall benefit of ratings systems, going beyond a simple list.
Secure (5-6 marks): Points on both sides with some application to the games industry and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided; limited engagement with the counter-argument.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic statements about ratings with no development or evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which organisation rates video games with age categories in the UK?
Which BBFC certificate is advisory rather than legally enforced at UK cinemas?
Copyright in a photograph, film or written work in the UK typically lasts for the creator's lifetime plus _____ years.
A _____ licence allows use of a copyrighted asset for a one-off payment with no ongoing fees each time it is published.
Match each term to its correct definition.
right: Pan European Game Information age rating system for video games
Oversimplified generalisations about groups of people repeated in media
The automatic legal right to control how an original work is used

flashcard_questions.a: The automatic legal right of a creator to control how their original work is used, copied or distributed.

flashcard_questions.q: When does copyright in a UK creative work typically expire?
flashcard_questions.a: Seventy years after the creator's death.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five PEGI age rating categories?
flashcard_questions.a: PEGI uses five age rating categories: PEGI 3, PEGI 7, PEGI 12, PEGI 16 and PEGI 18, covering content from suitable-for-all to adults-only.

flashcard_questions.q: Which PEGI ratings are legally enforced in UK retail?
flashcard_questions.a: PEGI 12, 16 and 18 are all legally enforced at UK retail points of sale, meaning retailers must not sell these games to underage buyers.
Films and video works for cinema and home release.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a CC BY-NC Creative Commons licence allow?
flashcard_questions.a: Use with attribution, provided the work is not used for commercial purposes.
A signed agreement from a person allowing their image to be used in a media product in a specified way.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between royalty-free and public domain?
flashcard_questions.a: Royalty-free requires a one-off purchase fee; public domain has no copyright and is free to use without restriction.
The repeated use of oversimplified, generalised and often inaccurate images of particular groups that can reinforce prejudice.

flashcard_questions.q: Which BBFC certificate is legally enforced for cinema admission for under-12s?
flashcard_questions.a: 12A (no one under 12 may be admitted without an accompanying adult).

flashcard_questions.q: What UK legislation governs how photographs identifying individuals can be collected and used?
flashcard_questions.a: The Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR.
